GitHub Copilot AI Training: What the Opt-Out Actually Controls

Updated October 9, 2026: the April policy change is in effect. Here is how to check your training preference and distinguish it from the data needed to run Copilot.

I first came across the change on Hacker News. GitHub announced it on March 25, 2026, with an effective date of April 24. That date has passed. If you use an individual Copilot plan, the useful question now is whether your training preference matches how you want your code handled.

GitHub's announcement distinguishes code stored in a private repository from data sent through Copilot. The training policy covers interactions, including prompts, outputs, code snippets, and associated context. A private repository setting does not, by itself, decide how a Copilot interaction may be used.

Code sent as context can therefore fall within the policy. That does not mean every private repository, or every snippet sent to Copilot, has already been used to train a model.

What Exactly Gets Collected

The current GitHub documentation describes the training setting. The categories to pay attention to are:

  • Inputs: prompts and code context sent to Copilot (the code around your cursor, your comments, your questions in chat)
  • Outputs: suggestions Copilot generates and whether you accepted, modified, or rejected them
  • Code snippets: the actual code fragments that flow between you and Copilot during a session
  • Associated context: information supplied alongside a request. Review the current product documentation for the context each feature sends.

The distinction matters when reviewing a team's setup. Repository access controls, the data sent to a coding assistant, and permission to use interactions for training are separate controls.

Who Is Affected (and Who Isn’t)

GitHub's current documentation lists these individual plans:

  • Copilot Free users
  • Copilot Pro users
  • Copilot Pro+ and Copilot Max users

Not affected:

  • Copilot Business users
  • Copilot Enterprise users
  • These are governed by separate Data Protection Agreements that explicitly exclude training

Paying for an individual plan does not give it the same data terms as an organization-managed Business or Enterprise subscription. Check the actual license on the account you use for work.

How to Opt Out of GitHub Copilot AI Training

Check the account you actually use in your editor:

  1. Go to github.com/settings/copilot
  2. Under Privacy, find “Allow GitHub to use my data for AI model training”
  3. Set it to Disabled

GitHub's March announcement said existing opt-outs from the relevant product-improvement setting would be preserved. Check the current setting rather than assuming a fresh opt-out is needed.

Disabling training use is not the same as disabling all service processing or requesting deletion of historical data. The setting does not establish whether a past interaction was used in a model, or reverse any training that has already happened.

Why I Wanted a Different Default

The part that bothered me was having to check a new use of data in a tool already embedded in my working day. A developer can reasonably notice a feature update before noticing a change to its data terms.

For me, three distinctions matter:

1. Training preference versus service operation. I want to make a deliberate choice about training use. Disabling it does not mean Copilot can operate without receiving the context I send to the service.

2. Individual versus organization-managed plans. A personal subscription is not a substitute for checking an employer's approved tools and contractual requirements. The price of the subscription does not settle that question.

3. Interaction data can contain code. The label is broader than source files, but prompts and context can still contain proprietary material. I review what a tool receives, not just what the setting is called.

The GDPR Question

A product opt-out does not, on its own, settle whether a particular use of personal data complies with data-protection law. That depends on the data, the purpose, the applicable legal basis, and the safeguards.

Legitimate interests is not automatic permission to process data. The ICO describes a purpose test, a necessity test, and a balancing test against the individual’s rights and interests. Consent is not the only possible legal basis, and an opt-out model alone does not establish illegality.

Proprietary code and personal data are not interchangeable categories. Code may contain personal data, but confidentiality, intellectual-property rights, and customer contracts can raise separate questions even when it does not.

I cannot determine the legal outcome of a hypothetical challenge from this policy announcement. For a company decision, the useful inputs are the current terms, the actual data flow, and the obligations attached to the code.

I'm based in Berlin and work with code owned by other organizations. I opted out because I wanted to limit training use. That is my preference, not a legal conclusion about every Copilot deployment.

For work covered by customer agreements or confidentiality terms, review the setup with the people responsible for those obligations. Include the account's license, the context being sent, and the applicable contractual terms.

What I’m Doing

I've opted out of training use. I still treat sending code to an external service as a separate decision.

Beyond that:

Auditing what flows through Copilot. I’m more conscious now about what context Copilot sees. If I’m working on security-sensitive code (auth, encryption, API keys in config), I consider whether I want that flowing through any external service, regardless of training policies.

Evaluating alternatives for sensitive projects. I would compare where inference runs, what leaves the machine, retention, training terms, and access controls. A tool's marketing label or an option to connect a local model is not enough to answer all of those questions.

The Bigger Picture

Coding assistants make it easy to send useful context without stopping to inspect each request. That convenience is why the data settings deserve a place in a team's setup checklist.

For me, the practical question is the same across tools: which service receives this code, under which account and terms, and for what purposes? A clear answer matters more than assuming that a paid plan or a private repository covers everything.

The opt-out is the minimum. The real question is whether you’re comfortable with any external service processing your most sensitive code, and whether the productivity gains justify that trust.

Open your Copilot settings and check the training preference. April 24 was the policy's effective date, not a reason to assume it is too late to change your preference now.

Further Reading

  • GitHub Changelog: Privacy Statement and ToS Updates
  • GitHub Blog: Copilot Interaction Data Usage Policy
  • GitHub: March 2026 policy announcement
  • The Register: GitHub Will Train on Your Data
  • InfoQ: GitHub Will Use Copilot Data from Free/Pro/Pro+ Users
  • dev.to: GitHub Copilot Is Training on Your Private Code Now
  • HN Discussion: If You Don’t Opt Out by April 24

I’m Burak Hamuryen, a Senior Software Engineer in Berlin with 14+ years of experience building distributed systems, real-time video processing, and cloud-native platforms. More at hamuryen.com.
